raw_response:
I am a 75-year-old woman. I have farmed these 3 mu of land in Quzhou for 50 years, since I was a young bride. My husband passed on ten years ago, and now I live alone. My children moved to Shijiazhuang for factory work. They send a little money, but I am proud and do not like to ask. These 3 mu of cotton are my own income.

At my age, I cannot carry heavy loads or work from dawn to dark like I once did. My back aches when I bend too long. But my mind is sharp, and I know every corner of these fields. I know where the soil is a little sandy, where water collects after rain, and which patch always flowers first.

**My plan for this year:**

I will plant cotton, as I always do. It is familiar. The cotton buyer still comes to our village in October, so I know I can sell it. I thought about giving up, but what else would I do with the land? Let it grow weeds?

I will plant around April 20th, when the apricot trees bloom. That is the signal I have always used. I hire Old Wang's son to bring his small tractor for rotary tillage — 40 yuan per mu. I cannot turn the soil myself anymore. I pay him 120 yuan for the 3 mu. Then I rake the beds by hand, slowly, over two days. I use local cotton seed from the county supply store. I do not buy the expensive new hybrids. The regular seed costs about 25 yuan per mu, and I need roughly 1.5 kg per mu. I have been using this variety for years. It is reliable.

For fertilizer, I am careful with money. I spread about 400 kg of chicken manure from my yard per mu before tillage. That costs me nothing but my labor. Then I buy compound fertilizer (15-15-15) — one bag is 50 kg for about 150 yuan. I use half a bag per mu as base fertilizer, applied when I plant. That is 25 kg per mu. I do not usually topdress with urea anymore. The bags are heavy, and at my age, carrying them to the field is too much. So I rely on the base fertilizer and the manure. I know this means my yield will not be the highest in the village, but it is what I can manage.

I will irrigate twice. The first time is right after planting if the spring is dry, which it often is now. The second time is at flowering in mid-July, the critical time. Pumping costs 18 yuan per mu each time, so two times on 3 mu is about 110 yuan. I do not water more because each time costs money, and walking the furrows to check the flow tires me out.

Pesticides I cannot skip. Cotton bollworm comes every year like a bad relative. I spray three times: once in early June for weeds and early insects, once in July when the bolls are forming, and once in August if I see aphids. I buy the generic insecticide and herbicide from the village store. Each spray costs about 15 yuan per mu, including the chemical and hiring young Liu to carry the sprayer tank. I cannot lift a full sprayer on my back anymore.

Labor is my biggest worry. I do the light work — checking plants, weeding around the roots by hand, collecting the picked cotton into bags. But for the heavy picking, I must hire women from the village. Cotton picking takes three or four rounds from September to October. For 3 mu, I need about 15 to 18 days of picking labor. I pay them 80 yuan per day, plus I cook them lunch. That is my largest expense, but there is no choice. My fingers cramp after half an hour of picking now.

I expect about 240 kg of seed cotton per mu this year. Last year I got 235, the year before 250. I am not using as much fertilizer as some, and I water less, so I do not expect more. But 240 kg per mu on 3 mu, sold at about 7.5 yuan per kg, gives me roughly 5,400 yuan. After paying for seed, fertilizer, irrigation, pesticide, machinery, and hired labor, I will have a little left. It is not much, but it is mine, and it is enough to live on with what my children send.
